extracted.intended_audience: researchers and science-communication professionals (press officers, health journalists, science communication scholars)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating exaggeration in health press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analysis protocol for comparing university press releases, their associated peer-reviewed journal articles, and resulting news stories to identify exaggeration in (1) advice to change behaviour, (2) causal claims from correlational research, and (3) inference to humans from non-human studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main outcome measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to readers to change behaviour, causal statements drawn from correlational research, and inference to humans from animal research that went beyond those in the associated peer reviewed papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three categories were the focus of analysis and form the primary outcomes for identifying exaggeration in press releases and news relative to the journal article baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice coding (four levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum level of advice coded using four levels based on explicitness and directness: no advice; implicit advice (e.g. 'these findings suggest that...'); explicit advice, but not to the reader/public (e.g. 'should be incorporated into everyday clinical practice'); explicit advice to the reader or general public (e.g. 'children who are thirsty should be encouraged to drink water').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each level. Relevant samples for analysis included any item containing at least one implicit or explicit advice statement in the journal article, press release, or news. Coding searched entire items for advice statements (n values given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal statements from correlational results (seven-point determinism scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: A seven-point scale rating increasing levels of determinism where stronger statements trump weaker ones: no statement; explicit statement of no relation; correlational (e.g. 'drinking wine is associated with increased cancer rates'); ambiguous (e.g. 'drinking wine linked to cancer risk'); conditional causal (e.g. 'drinking wine might increase cancer risk'); 'can cause' (e.g. 'drinking wine can increase cancer risk'); and unconditionally causal (e.g. 'drinking wine increases cancer risk').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied only to correlational research (observational cross-sectional and longitudinal designs); qualitative, interventional, or simulation designs were excluded. For press releases and news the title and first two sentences were used as the main statements; for journal articles the abstract and discussion were used. The first claim statement was used for the primary analysis; secondary statements about different variable pairs were also coded for replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions for humans from non-human studies (three-level coding)
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-human studies (animals, cells, or simulations) code whether the main statements were phrased as explicitly non-human, implicitly human (e.g. 'a pregnant mother’s stress level affects the brain of her unborn baby'), or explicitly human (e.g. 'a pregnant woman’s stress ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For journal articles the discussion section and abstract were searched for statements about human relevance. Relevant samples and examples are reported; these codes were used to detect inflated inference to humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats and justifications coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Search the whole press release and news stories for any caveats stated for the advice, causal claims, or inference to humans (e.g. 'This is a population study. It cannot say definitively that...') and for any justifications that would help readers judge which statements are warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats and justifications were noted and later analysed for association with news uptake and exaggeration. Examples given; caveats were rare in press releases in this sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of exaggeration (comparison baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking the peer reviewed journal article as the baseline, instances where press releases or news offered advice, causal claims, or human inferences that went beyond (or were more direct/stronger than) those in the associated journal article were considered exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note this does not assume journal articles are true or optimally phrased; some journal articles may themselves be exaggerated, meaning measured exaggeration may be an underestimate. Exaggeration was operationalised separately for advice, causal determinism, and human inference categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of main statements for coding
rubrics_metrics.description: For press releases and news the title and first two sentences were used as their main statements; for journal articles the abstract and discussion were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: nearly all press releases and news follow the 'inverted pyramid' structure stating main claims first. This selection method was used consistently when coding main statements for causal inference and human inference measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of correlational research inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlational research defined as observational cross-sectional and longitudinal designs; only these were included for analysis of causal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative, interventional, or simulation designs were excluded from causal-claim analyses. The difficulty of inferring causation from correlational data is emphasised as motivation for the stricter focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample inclusion criteria and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases based on published studies with possible relevance for human health (biomedical and psychological sciences) issued in 2011 by the 20 Russell Group UK universities; associated peer-reviewed journal articles and national print/online news stories (broadcast news excluded) were identified and coded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers: 462 press releases, 668 news stories. The sample choice rationale and limitations (Russell Group, 2011) are documented. Source searches included Nexis, BBC, Reuters, and Google.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding reliability and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Each set took on average 3–4 hours to code. Double coding was performed on 27% of press releases and journal articles and 21% of news stories, with concordance rate 91% and mean κ=0.88.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the large numbers, simulations showed 10% disagreement would not influence conclusions. Full coding sheets (n=462), instructions, and data files are available online for transparency and replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study facts and quotes coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Coders recorded facts about the study and press release, including sample size, duration, completion rate, and the source of quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These variables were analysed separately (supplementary sections cited) and used to corroborate press release as a source of content in news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs secondary statement coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary analysis focused on the first claim statement; where a second statement occurred about a different variable pair, it was also coded for replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule ensured consistency in selecting which claim to compare across journal article, press release, and news for the primary outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis choices for evaluating association
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of generalised estimating equations to calculate percentages and 95% confidence intervals for news with exaggeration relative to the journal article, adjusting for clustering of several news articles to one press release; odds ratios estimated for association between PR exaggeration and news exaggeration; bootstrapped 95% CIs used for some comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the analytical standards used to assess whether PR exaggeration was associated with higher rates of news exaggeration or increased news uptake; guidance on interpretation (correlational design limits causal inference) is provided.
